Delegates and visiting brothers will find register and information
bureau in lobby of Clift Hotel on arrival, September 1. Identification
ribbons, banquet tickets, and programs can be secured here. Accommo
dations have been reserved at the above hotel for the convention period.
For the benefit of those who are unable to attend the barbecue on the
flrst official day, arrangements have been made to meet informally at Alt

Hotel Osburn
Eugene, Oregon
Sept. 1st, 1915
My dear Mr. Bridgman:
I have just emerged from my summer sojourn in the forest's
and mountains of Oregon. I regret most sincerely the impossibility
of my joining the Psi U brothers in San Francisco, my duties
calling me quite the opposite direction�
to Portland and Seattle�

thing most dear to my deceased and honored

Most Fraternally Yours,

Phi Kappa Society. The petition of the Phi Kappa Society of the
University of Washington for a charter of Psi Upsilon has again failed
to secure approval of the Chapters. The negative votes of the Upsilon
and the Chi disposed of the application for the present year. The Tau
voted 15 to 9 in favor of the application (one short of the two-thirds
vote required). No reports were received from the Theta, Delta, Beta,
Lambda, Kappa, Phi or Epsilon. The remaining chapters voted favorably
on the application.
Chapter Address Lists. The convention of 1913 by general resolu
tion No. 1 directed the Council to publish a first edition of Chapter
Address Lists of members of the Fraternity. The Coimcil appointed
Brother William P. MacCracken, Jr. (Omega '09), of Chicago, as Chief
Master of the Rolls, without salary, and the edition based on data
furnished by the several chapters has been printed and mailed. A bound
set of all the lists was sent to each chapter. The cost of this work
at $825.27 has been paid and the question of a new edition has been
considered. A card index prepared for the work has been corrected in
an endeavor to overcome the large percentage (nearly 20 per cent.) of
errors and this index is being kept up to date as information is received.
While there are many typographical mistakes some
chapters suffered
more than others from erroneous addresses, indicating defects in the
original data supplied. The result seems to show the need of a standard
list for all chapters, compiled, kept as
nearly correct as possible and
handled by one printer. The printer previously selected (the only one
making a specialty of college fraternity work), is being favorably con
sidered. He has the type standing, has the experience of the first
edition, and his rather disadvantageous location is offset by economy of
operation as shown by bids secured from New York printers. A new
and corrected edition will probably cost (exclusive of postage) about half
as much as the flrst. It is recommended that the Council be authorized
to publish new editions from time to time as it may deem desirable.
New General Catalogue. The latest General Catalogue of the
Fraternity was published in 1902. A supplement containing the names

19
of member's subsequently admitted was published in 1908. There is no
general catalogue containing the members of classes from 1906 to 1918
inclusive. The eighth do-decade of the Fraternity begins with the year
1917, and it would seem proper at this time to consider the propriety of
preparing for a twelfth edition of the General Catalogue, to be published
as early as practicable in 1917.
The Psi Upsilon Epitome. From time to time requests are made
to the Council for copies of the Psi Upsilon Epitome published in 1884
by Brother Albert Poole Jacobs, Phi '73. The Council has never had
copies for distribution, the work having been prepared by Brother Jacobs
personally and sold by him. It covers the first half century of the
Fraternity and is full of interest. The Council recommends that it be
authorized to publish a reprint of the Epitome if it shall find that a
sufficient demand exists, to present five copies to each chapter, and to
sell copies to members of the Fraternity at as low a price as practicable.
The Council further recommends that it be authorized to consider
the propriety of publishing a new volume of Fraternity Annals bringing
the Epitome down to date, the proposition to be submitted to and
approved by the Chapters before any financial responsibility is assumed.
Comparative Chapter Standing. There will be submitted to the
Convention the report of a committee appointed by the President of the
Executive Council to formulate a system for a basis of comparison among
the chapters to indicate their relative standing in scholarship and
undergraduate activities in the colleges where Psi Upsilon is established.
Upon the coming in of the report printed copies were sent to a number
of representative alumni of the chapters for an expression of their views
either as to the scheme as a whole or as to particular details. The replies
received were forwarded to a member of the committee for comment and
the replies and comments accompany the printed copy of the report to be
submitted herewith.
Old Omega Archives. The Omega Chapter has requested that the
constitution and archives of the Old Omega, which were transmitted to
the Council when the old Chicago University closed its doors, be sent to
the new chapter of the same name in the new university. The Council
recommends this disposition, provided the Convention approve and the
members of the Old Omega consent.

20
Sectional Conferences of Chapters. By General Resolution No. 3
of the convention of 1914 it was "Resolved, That so for as possible and
convenient the chapters in the same section of the country endeavor to
hold periodical conferences." The discussion in the Convention brought
out very clearly that such gatherings were to be in no sense legislative,
but were to be purely social and fraternal meetings, to foster friendly
acquaintance and intercourse and the interchange of views for mutual
benefit. It is hoped that the chapters generally will avail themselves of
the opportunity of fostering these relations.
Visitation of Chapters. Formal visits have been made during the
year to the Delta, Beta, Kappa, Pi, Beta Beta and Eta, and informal
visits to the Theta, Xi and Delta Delta.
Business Information. The report of the Committee on Business
Information, received from Brother Earl D. Babst, Phi '93, its Chairman,
is submitted as part of this communication.
Treasurer's Report. The report of the Treasurer is submitted
herewith.
The Council. The officers of the Council for the past year have
been the same as for the previous year. Twelve regular meetings have
been held and copies of the minutes distributed as usual.
The terms of Brother Wertheimer (Iota '99) and Brother Whiting
(Tau '88) expire with this Convention, and two members are to be elected
for the term ending in 1920.
The Council takes pleasure in reporting that the Chapters as a
whole have maintained the improvements noted a
year ago; that the
Alumni Associations have shown a growing interest in Fraternity affairs;
and that the members of Psi Upsilon have continued to hold an honorable
place in the affairs of city, state and nation.

and best wishes on the occasion of their flrst Convention, which officially
demonstrates that the West and the East are one.

(APPENDIX A2)
Report of Committee on Comparative Chapter Standing
To THE Executive Council of the
Psi Upsilon Fraternity:
At a meeting of the Executive Council of the Psi Upsilon Fraternity,
June 8, 1914, the following resolution was passed:
Resolved that the President appoint a Committee of two members of
the Council and four other members of the Fraternity to formulate and
present to the Council, not later than the December meeting, a
system
for a basis of comparison among the Chapters of the Fraternity to indicate
now, and from year to year in the future, their relative standing in
scholarship, college influence, showing their comparative ability in
athletics, public speaking, music, journalism, drama, as well as other
undergraduate activities in the colleges and universities where Psi
Upsilon has chapters.
Pursuant to this resolution, the following committee was appointed:
Professor Walter P. Willcox, Oamma, of Cornell University.
Doctor Charles T. Burnett, Oamma, of Bowdoin College.
Mr. Frederick P. Keppel, Lambda, Dean of Columbia College and
member of the Executive Council.
Mr. Theodore L. Waugh, Pi, attorney-at-law of New York City and
member of the Executive Council.
Mr. John H. MacCracken, Delta, President-elect of Lafayette College,
Easton, Pa.
Mr. Homer Eaton Keyes, Zeta, Business Director of Dartmouth
College.
On November 9th, the Committee was enlarged to seven by the
appointment of Doctor Frank Hoyt Wood, Pi, Professor of American
History, Hamilton College, Clinton, N. Y.
Meetings were held in the rooms of the Psi Upsilon Club in New
York City on June 29th and November 16th, 1914, at which the members
were present.

23
As a result of these conferences, and of subsequent correspondence
among the members of the Committee, we, the undersigned, beg to present
a preliminary draft of such a system as that called for in the resolution,
together with some comment, and with recommendation as to further
procedure.
We believe it possible to show approximately the standing and condi
tion of each Chapter as compared with the other Chapters constituting
the Psi Upsilon Fraternity, and, furthermore, as compared with the
activities of the student body among whom any Chapter exists.
The underlying principle of such a comparison -should, in our opinion,
be that of following at the outset all the lines of endeavor and achieve
ment, as well as excellence of conduct, which, in any degree, constituta
the undergraduate interests in the college of today. This should be done,
furthermore, without making any immediate attempt to emphasize the
value of one such line over another. Later on, and as experience dictates,
the activities which seem to the Committee to possess most permanent
value, may properly be emphasized with a view to centering a larger
measure of student attention upon them.
We take it as conceded that the college fraternity system in general,
and the active membership of Psi Upsilon in particular, stand to be
benefited rather than injured by any intelligent attempt, however incom
plete, to stimulate undergraduate accomplishment by instituting com
parisons between Chapters.
One immediate result should be increased unity of idea throughout
the Fraternity by virtue of the recognition of certain common standards
of attainment which all the Chapters should strive to meet. Encourage
ment to sustained effort will be afforded through the principle of com
petition, whose value in modern business and professional organization is
too well understood to require defense from us.
Beyond this, it may well be hoped that the arousing of active ambi
tion in the various groups may have an
equally beneficial effect upon the
individuals constituting them. If so, one of Psi Upsilon's objects,
mutual assistance, may acquire a new and really practical meaning in a
large and effective way.
Because of our
hopes of the ultimate development and value of an
annual comparison and grading of all the twenty-three Chapters, we

24
advise a slow and careful launching of any system of measurement.
We cannot find that it has been used to full possibilities by any one
fraternity or any one college. Because of the formative nature of the
project, we suggest one
year's preliminary trial of a
reporting system
in conjunction with the Annual Report. Under the Council's power of
visitation and supervision, cannot a "survey" of one calendar year be
made which will furnish not only experience and knowledge, but will
be a test of the value of comparison as a stimulus to action?
Psi Upsilon's policy of expecting the free and voluntary rendering
of personal services by its members when called to her assistance, will
minimize the cost of such a survey to postage and slight expenditures
for printing and letter writing. The availability of alumni and brethren
in the faculties of nearly every university, will reduce traveling expenses
to such as the Council shall expressly authorize.
As a means of securing the data necessary to a
comparison of Chapter
records, the Committee has prepared and herewith submits a proposed
form of blank. A copy of this blank should, we believe, be forwarded to
each Chapter as an integral part of the existing form of required Chapter
report, and returned at a
specified date to a designated secretary.
A temporary committee should examine the data provided, and, on
the basis of these, make an attempt to grade the Chapters.
The flrst experiment in this direction will necessarily be not wholly
satisfactory. It will, however, afford the exeperience indispensable to the
preparation of a really adequate questionnaire, and, what is more im
portant, will give a needful understanding of the student viewpoint in a
number of widely scattered institutions.
A year later, a more permanent alumni committee should be estab
lished and the appraising of what is worth while in the Chapters of Psi
Upsilon on the basis not of subjective impression, but of objective demon
stration, seriously and methodically undertaken.
It should be fairly clear that the proposed procedure will be of benefit
not only in stimulating the ambition of each Chapter to rank well among
its fellows of the same
Fraternity, but in educating each Chapter to
valuable introspection. The adequate filling of the proposed blank will
necessitate careful appraisal of a
Chapter by its own
membership. In
analyzing its own record and defining its own
achievement, it cannot

25
well avoid an
approach at least to truer standards of value than now
frequently obtain.
We accordingly recommend as follows:
I. That the attempt be made, for a period of years, to institute an
annual grading of the Chapters of Psi Upsilon for the purpose of
showing their relative standing as indicated by the character and ability
of their undergraduate members.
II. That the form herewith submitted be used in obtaining informa
tion upon which to base the grading above mentioned.
III. That the said form be sent to the various Chapters in conjunc
tion with, and as part of, the material for Annual Chapter Reports.
IV. That a special committee be appointed to pass upon these reports
as submitted by the Chapters, to grade the Chapters on the basis of
their reports and to publish this grading to the Fraternity in such way
as
may seem best to the committee.
V. That this committee be authorized to make, from time to time,
'such changes as it may deem necessary in the form of questionnaire to
be sent to the various Chapters of the Fraternity.
VI. That the committee be appointed annually by the Council, so
long as it may seem desirable to continue the procedure above outlined.
Respectfully submitted,
Walter F. Willcox
Charles T. Burnett
Frederick P. Keppel
